title: Basketball in the Neighborhood
bigQuestion: How did Ys, settlement houses, parks and dance halls give city kids and adults rooms to play basketball before television?

story.title: A Chain Net in the Alley
story.kicker: A court painted on an alley floor has a long history behind it.
paragraphs: Behind a row of brick two-flats on Chicago's West Side, a metal hoop hangs on a garage wall. Its net is made of chain, not string. A string net would rot in the rain and snow. The chain one clanks every time the ball drops through, and it lasts for years.

The alley is also a road. Cars pass through, and the players step aside. Chalk marks show where the lane would be. Nobody sold a ticket. Nobody wrote a schedule. Yet the players follow rules everyone in the city seems to know.

The game did not start in alleys. It was invented in a YMCA gym in Springfield, Massachusetts, in 1891. From there it spread to settlement houses, park field houses, church basements and dance halls. Each room was built by a group with its own reasons: faith, reform, city government or business.

A few miles east is Hull House, where Jane Addams opened a settlement in 1889. Its gym was one of the first public places on the West Side where immigrant children could play indoors. This chapter follows the ball from those rooms to the playground hoop.
story.think: Who pays for a court in your neighborhood, and who decides who may use it?

lessons.title: Hull House on Halsted Street
lessons.mainIdea: Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr opened Hull House in Chicago in 1889, and its gym gave immigrant neighbors indoor space to play.
reading: In 1889 Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr moved into an old mansion on Halsted Street in Chicago. The neighborhood was crowded with immigrants from Italy, Greece, Russia, Ireland and many other places. Families lived in small, dark rooms. Children played in the streets because there was nowhere else.

Hull House was a *settlement house*. Educated reformers settled, or lived, in a poor neighborhood to work beside their neighbors. Hull House offered classes, a kindergarten, a library, a theater and clubs. In the 1890s it added a gymnasium building.

The gym was used by boys' clubs, girls' clubs and adult classes. Basketball, a new game, fit its small floor well. For many children it was their first chance to play a team game indoors, in winter, with an adult who kept order.

words.d: a center in a poor neighborhood where reformers lived and ran classes, clubs and services
a person who moves to a new country to live
a person who works to change and improve society

lessons.title: A Movement from London
lessons.mainIdea: The settlement idea began at Toynbee Hall in London in 1884 and spread to American cities such as Chicago and New York.
reading: The first settlement house was *Toynbee Hall*, opened in East London in 1884. Young university men lived there to learn about and serve the poor. Jane Addams visited Toynbee Hall in the 1880s. She brought the idea home to Chicago.

Other American settlements followed quickly. In New York, Lillian Wald founded the Henry Street Settlement in 1893, starting with nursing care. In Chicago, Graham Taylor founded Chicago Commons in 1894. Hundreds of settlements opened in American cities by the early 1900s.

Many settlements built gyms or used nearby halls for games. Reformers believed team games taught fairness, teamwork and self-control. Some also hoped games would keep boys away from gangs and saloons. Settlement teams played one another, making early city leagues.

words.d: the first settlement house, opened in East London in 1884
many people working together over time toward the same change

lessons.title: Jane Addams on Youth and Play
lessons.mainIdea: In 1909 Jane Addams argued that cities must give young people safe places for play instead of leaving them to the streets.
reading: In 1909 Jane Addams published a book called *The Spirit of Youth and the City Streets*. She wrote about the young workers of Chicago. Many left school early and worked long hours in factories and shops. At night they looked for fun in cheap theaters and dance halls.

Addams argued that the wish to play was healthy, not a problem to punish. The problem was that the city offered young people so little. She said a city should provide parks, playgrounds and gyms, just as it provided schools. Play, she wrote, was a public duty.

Her book helped build support for public *recreation*, meaning free-time activity provided for everyone. Addams later won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1931. She was the first American woman to receive it.

words.d: free-time activity for fun and health, often provided by a city

lessons.title: Chicago's Park Field Houses
lessons.mainIdea: In 1905 Chicago's South Park Commission opened neighborhood parks with field houses that held gyms, baths and meeting rooms.
reading: Chicago's big parks, like Washington Park, were far from the crowded neighborhoods near the stockyards and mills. In 1905 the South Park Commission opened a set of new, smaller neighborhood parks. They were designed by the Olmsted Brothers and the firm of Daniel Burnham.

Each park had a *field house*. It held indoor gyms for men and women, showers and baths, a library branch, and meeting rooms. Outside were ball fields, running tracks and playgrounds. Visitors came from other cities to study them. President Theodore Roosevelt praised them.

The field houses made the city itself a sponsor of play. Neighborhood teams practiced and played basketball in their gyms. In 1934, Chicago joined its 22 separate park districts into one *Chicago Park District*. It still runs field houses across the city.

words.d: a park building with gyms, baths and meeting rooms for the neighborhood
the city body, formed in 1934, that runs Chicago's parks and field houses

lessons.title: The Playground Movement
lessons.mainIdea: The Playground Association of America, founded in 1906, pushed cities to build public playgrounds and hire people to run them.
reading: By the early 1900s many reformers agreed that cities needed places to play. In 1906 they founded the *Playground Association of America*. Its leaders included Luther Gulick, Joseph Lee of Boston and Jane Addams. Its first president was Gulick.

The association urged cities to build playgrounds near schools and homes. It also urged them to hire a trained *play leader* for each playground to run games and keep order. It held national meetings. In 1907 it met in Chicago, where visitors toured the new field houses.

The movement changed city budgets. Before it, play space was a gift from charities. After it, many cities paid for playgrounds with tax money, like schools and libraries. Outdoor hoops on playgrounds put basketball within walking distance of city kids.

words.d: a group founded in 1906 to get cities to build and run public playgrounds
a paid worker who ran games and kept order at a public playground

lessons.title: New York's School League
lessons.mainIdea: In 1903 Luther Gulick helped found New York's Public Schools Athletic League, which brought basketball into city school sport.
reading: Luther Gulick ran the YMCA training school in Springfield where basketball began. In 1903 he became director of physical training for New York City's public schools. That year he helped found the *Public Schools Athletic League*, or PSAL.

The PSAL organized contests for boys across the city's schools. Basketball was one of its sports, because a school gym or even a hall could hold a game. In 1905 a Girls' Branch was formed. It favored dance and games inside schools over public contests between schools.

The PSAL showed that a city school system could run sports for thousands of children. It was supported by wealthy donors as well as the city. It became a model for other cities. It also shows how the same reformers moved between the Y, the playground and the school.

words.d: New York City's school sports league, founded in 1903
an older name for school classes in exercise and games

lessons.title: Black Ys and E. B. Henderson
lessons.mainIdea: Shut out of many white Y branches, Black communities built their own Ys, and Edwin B. Henderson brought organized basketball to Black students in Washington.
reading: Many YMCA branches in the early 1900s did not admit Black members. Black communities built their own branches. In Chicago, the *Wabash Avenue YMCA* opened in 1913 on the South Side. Its building was paid for partly by the businessman Julius Rosenwald and by Black donors in Chicago.

Edwin Bancroft Henderson was a Black teacher from Washington, D.C. He learned basketball in a summer course at Harvard. Around 1904 he began teaching the game to Black students in Washington's segregated schools. He also organized teams and a league among Black schools and clubs.

Henderson is often called the grandfather of Black basketball. The Black Ys and school leagues he helped build gave players rooms, coaches and schedules. Those were the rooms that white-run leagues refused to open to them. Later Black pro teams drew many players from them.

words.d: kept apart by race, by law or by custom
a YMCA for Black Chicagoans, opened on the South Side in 1913

lessons.title: The Rens and the Ballroom Court
lessons.mainIdea: The New York Renaissance, founded in 1923 by Bob Douglas, played in a Harlem ballroom and won the first world pro tournament in 1939.
reading: In 1923 Robert "Bob" Douglas founded a Black professional team in Harlem. He named it after the *Renaissance Casino*, a ballroom where the team played its home games. Fans came for basketball and stayed for dancing when the game ended. The floor served both.

The Rens were barred from the white pro leagues of the time. So they spent much of each season *barnstorming*, or touring for a share of the gate. They played white teams and Black teams in towns across the country. Many hotels and restaurants refused them, so they often slept and ate on their own team bus.

In 1939 the Chicago Herald-American newspaper held the first *World Professional Basketball Tournament* in Chicago. It was open to Black and white teams. The Rens won it. In 1963 the whole team was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame.

words.d: traveling from town to town to play games for a share of the ticket money
a tournament held in Chicago from 1939, open to Black and white pro teams

lessons.title: Neighborhood Teams Go Pro
lessons.mainIdea: Community teams like the SPHAS in Philadelphia and the Globetrotters from Chicago grew out of neighborhood clubs and halls into pro teams.
reading: In 1918 Eddie Gottlieb and friends in Philadelphia started a team linked to the South Philadelphia Hebrew Association. The team was called the *SPHAS*. It began as a club for young Jewish men in a mostly immigrant neighborhood. It grew into one of the best pro teams of the 1930s.

The SPHAS often played on Saturday nights in a hotel ballroom, with dancing after the game. Their fans came from the neighborhood. Gottlieb later helped found the NBA's Philadelphia Warriors. His career shows how a neighborhood club could turn into a business.

In Chicago, Abe Saperstein began managing a team of Black players from the South Side in the late 1920s. It became the *Harlem Globetrotters*, even though it was from Chicago. The team barnstormed across the Midwest. It won the World Professional Basketball Tournament in 1940.

words.d: a Philadelphia team, started in 1918, named for the South Philadelphia Hebrew Association
a touring team of Black players started in Chicago in the late 1920s

lessons.title: College Nights at the Garden
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1930s promoter Ned Irish filled Madison Square Garden with college doubleheaders, and the NIT began there in 1938.
reading: In the early 1930s college basketball was played mostly in small campus gyms. Ned Irish, a New York sportswriter, saw that fans were turned away at the doors. In December 1934 he rented Madison Square Garden for a *doubleheader*, two college games on one night.

More than 16,000 people came. Irish held many more doubleheaders. Teams traveled from across the country to play in New York. In 1938 the Metropolitan Basketball Writers Association started the *National Invitation Tournament*, or NIT, at the Garden.

The Garden turned college basketball into a big-city show sold to the public. The NCAA started its own tournament in 1939. For years the NIT was seen as the more important of the two. The game had moved from the settlement gym to an arena built for boxing.

words.d: two games played one after the other on the same day or night
a college basketball tournament begun at Madison Square Garden in 1938

lessons.title: Outdoor Courts and the Chain Net
lessons.mainIdea: Outdoor city courts with metal backboards and chain nets became free public rooms where players built their own leagues and reputations.
reading: Outdoor hoops spread with the playground movement. City parks and schoolyards put up metal poles and backboards. String nets wore out fast in wind, sun and snow. Many cities hung a *chain net*, which lasted for years and made a sound players recognized.

An outdoor court was free and open most hours. No one needed a club membership or a ticket. Players made their own rules for who played next and how long a game lasted. A player's name could spread across a city through word of mouth alone.

In Harlem, a parks worker named Holcombe Rucker started a summer tournament around 1950. He wanted to keep young people busy and pushed them to stay in school. The *Rucker* tournament later drew college and pro players to a small park court. It showed that the open court could become an institution too.

words.d: a basketball net made of metal chain, used on outdoor courts because it lasts
the Harlem summer tournament started by parks worker Holcombe Rucker
